title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus via MVT Structure (OQ-04)
description: Establishes the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and shows how MVT is the local/discrete counterpart to FTC's global/integral structure. Proves: FTC first and second forms, MVT as a consequence, and the precise connection: FTC = quantitative average of MVT pointwise bounds. 14 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) states: if F is antiderivative of f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a). The Mean Value Theorem (MVT) states: F(b) − F(a) = F'(c) · (b−a) for some c ∈ (a,b). The FTC is the 'global' version of MVT: instead of one value F'(c), it uses the integral average ∫f = (1/(b-a))·∫f(x)dx as the 'mean value'.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize FTC and MVT, and prove the structural connection: FTC is the exact version while MVT gives an existential point, and the two are related by the mean value interpretation.
overview.proofStrategy: FTC: use Mathlib's intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt. MVT: Mathlib's exists_deriv_eq_slope. Connection: f(b)-f(a) = ∫f'dt = mean(f') · (b-a), while MVT gives f(b)-f(a) = f'(c) · (b-a) for some c.
keyInsights: **FTC-MVT duality**: FTC says f(b)-f(a) = ∫ₐᵇ f'(t)dt (exact). MVT says f(b)-f(a) = f'(c)(b-a) (existential). FTC gives the true average; MVT says the average is attained somewhere.
**Mean value interpretation**: ∫ₐᵇ f'(t)dt / (b-a) = 'average' of f'. MVT: this average equals f'(c) for some c — the average is achieved.
**Integral Mean Value Theorem**: ∃ c ∈ [a,b], f(c) = (1/(b-a)) ∫ₐᵇ f(t)dt — the integral mean is attained by continuous functions.

sections.title: FTC, MVT, and their Structural Connection
sections.summary: FTC_first_form, FTC_second_form, MVT, integral_mean_value. Connection: FTC_implies_MVT and MVT_FTC_duality.
sections.mathContext: FTC: $f(b)-f(a) = \int_a^b f'(t)\,dt$. MVT: $f(b)-f(a) = f'(c)(b-a)$ for some $c \in (a,b)$.

conclusion.summary: FTC-MVT structural connection: 14 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: The formal connection between FTC and MVT clarifies why both theorems are 'about the same thing' — the difference quotient. FTC gives the exact answer; MVT gives an existential sample point.
openQuestions: Can the higher-dimensional MVT (gradient form) be connected to Stokes' theorem?
Can the Cauchy MVT be formalized and related to L'Hôpital's rule?
Can the connection between MVT and Taylor's theorem be made explicit in Lean?
